region.text: the Surat factory, the Company's first permanent Indian base (a factory in a Mughal city, one grid cell, not ceded land)

ledger.note: 1600: Elizabeth I's charter founds the East India Company. 'They convened again a year later, on 31 December 1600, and this time they succeeded' (infobox 31 December 1600). The page puts the 'First Permanent Factory' at Surat in 1613 ('trading posts in Surat (1619) and Madras (1639)' elsewhere), so the map's first land is Surat from 1613 and the 1600-1612 core is the researcher's reading. A factory in a Mughal city is not territory: the single grid cell is the birth marker at the Company's first base, not land ceded to it (reviewer sa-06-x, 2026-10-25); the Company's first land by purchase or grant is Madras (1639).

region.text: Madrasapatnam and Fort St George

ledger.note: 1639: the Company buys Madras. 'In 1639, the East India Company purchased the village of Madrasapatnam' (elsewhere 'obtained in 1640'); the EIC page also dates 'Madras (1639)'. The page does not name the seller.

region.text: Bombay island

ledger.note: 1668: the Crown passes Bombay to the Company. 'In 1661 Bombay was ceded to the Kingdom of England as part of the dowry of the infanta Catherine of Braganza' (infobox 1662); in 1668 'transferred to the East India Company for an annual payment of GBP 10'; the Company's headquarters moved there in 1687.

region.text: Fort St David

ledger.note: 1690: Fort St David. The Madras page says it was 'acquired in 1690'; the seller is not named.

region.text: the Company's base at Calcutta

ledger.note: 1696: Fort William at Calcutta. 'The original fort was built in the year 1696 by the British East India Company' with permission 'granted by Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb' (no year), 'named after King William III in 1700'. The EIC page says only that after the 1690 surrender the Company 'set up a new base in Calcutta' (no year); the Fort William page is silent on 1690, Job Charnock and the zamindari grant of 1698, so 1696 is the first dated land. Reviewer sa-06-x thin finding, 2026-10-25: the first version bridged 1690 at confidence 1.

region.text: the land within the Maratha Ditch and 600 yards beyond it and the zamindari between Calcutta and the sea

ledger.note: 23 June 1757: Plassey. Under the treaty with Mir Jafar 'the British acquired all the land within the Maratha Ditch and 600 yards (550 m) beyond it', plus 'the zamindari of all the land between Calcutta and the sea'; infobox 'De facto beginning of the Company rule in India'. The page does not name the 24 Parganas.

region.text: the Nawab's Bengal and Bihar after Plassey

ledger.note: June 1757: Bengal and Bihar under a Company puppet. 'Clive placed Mir Jafar on the throne' at Murshidabad (29 June); the Company page: 'Battle of Plassey: 23 June 1757' opens its timeline. Drawn as a client tint until the diwani of 1765.

region.text: Masulipatnam, kept by the British after taking it from the French

ledger.note: 1759: Masulipatnam. After the conquest of Masulipatnam 'the maritime provinces from the river Gundlakamma to the Chilka Lake were transferred from the French to the British', but the British 'left most of them under the Nizam' and kept Masulipatnam only. The extract's heading gives 1759; the page says the Circars process ran 'from 1758 to 1823'.

ledger.note: 1760: Mir Qasim, installed 'with the support of the British East India Company', 'granted it the right to collect revenue of the districts of Burdwan, Midnapore and Chittagong'. The page gives no year for the grant; 1760 is his accession (20 October 1760).

region.text: the Nawab's Bengal and Bihar

ledger.note: 16 August 1765: the Nawab's Bengal ceases to be a plain client. The Company page: 'the Company was granted the diwani, or the right to collect revenue, in Bengal and Bihar'.

region.text: Bengal and Bihar under the Company's diwani (Bangladesh, West Bengal and Bihar)

ledger.note: 16 August 1765: the diwani of Bengal and Bihar. 'Alam granted the East India Company Diwani rights' over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa; the Company page: 'Treaty of Allahabad: 16 August 1765'. A nominal Nawab remained (Nizamat abolished 1773 on the Company page, 1793 on the Bengal Presidency and Mir Qasim pages); Orissa was not held until Cuttack in 1803. Allahabad and Kora went to Shah Alam II, not to the Company.

region.text: the Northern Circars: Chicacole, Rajahmundry, Ellore and Kondapalli, about 78,000 km2

ledger.note: 1768: the Nizam gives up the Northern Circars. The Treaty of Masulipatnam: the Nizam accepts Shah Alam's grant of 1765 (which Clive had obtained with the seizure of Kondapalli) and 'resigned the Circars to the British East India Company', for an annuity of GBP 50,000; the 12 November 1766 treaty of alliance came first. Guntur stayed with Basalat Jang.
1773: Calcutta becomes the Company's capital. 'abolished local rule (Nizamat) in Bengal and established a capital in Calcutta' (timeline row 1773; infobox capital Calcutta).

region.text: Chatham Island in the south-east bay of Great Andaman, the 1789 naval base and penal colony (now Port Blair)

ledger.note: 1789: the Andaman settlement. 'In 1789, the Bengal Presidency established a naval base and penal colony on Chatham Island' in the south-east bay of Great Andaman (now Port Blair). A one-cell naval station, not the island group: the Andamanese held the islands and the Nicobars are on no Company page (they were Danish: danish-india). Reviewer sa-06-x, 2026-10-25: the first version drew the whole Andaman and Nicobar admin-1 as Company land from 1796 to 1858, the reverse of the page, which says the government 'ceased operating it in May 1796'.

region.text: Dindigul and its country, ceded by Tipu Sultan in 1792

'In 1790, James Stewart of the British army conquered Dindigul again during third war of Mysore' and 'In a pact made on 1792, Tipu ceded Dindigul to the British' (the page names neither the Company nor the Treaty of Seringapatam of 18 March 1792, which is the pact of that year). The circle is the researcher's reading of the district. The Baramahal, the other 1792 gain on the gap list, is on no page opened (the Baramahal page does not exist and the Krishnagiri district page is silent); the Salem circle of the Malabar gain stands in part for it.

'Salem and Malabar districts were obtained from Tipu Sultan in 1792 as per the Treaty of Seringapatam'; Third Anglo-Mysore War: 'On 18 March 1792, Tipu agreed to the terms and signed the Treaty of Seringapatam' and Cornwallis 'negotiated a division of one half of Mysorean territory, to be divided by the allies'. The Third War page names no ceded district; Dindigul and Baramahal are not on any page opened.

region.text: Kumaon and Garhwal east of the Alaknanda, the western Terai, and the strip east of the Mechi to the Teesta; Tehri Garhwal, left to its rajah, is not included

ledger.note: 4 March 1816: Sugauli. Nepal lost 'the territories of Kumaon and Garhwal and Western Terai', renounced land 'west of the Mahakali extending to the Sutlej' and 'east of the Mechi extending to the Teesta', and 'lost all Sikkim (including Darjeeling)'; the Company paid 200,000 rupees a year for the Terai and 'some of them were returned to the kingdom later in 1816'. The page does not say which Terai lands came back, so the western Terai is drawn whole. Tehri Garhwal is not Company land: the Garhwal Kingdom page says the British annexed 'the eastern half of the Garhwal region, which lies east of Alaknanda' and that Sudarshan Shah 'received approximately half his ancestral territories, limited to western Garhwal'; the Anglo-Nepalese War page's 'partly annexed by the company and partly restored to its previous rulers' says the same in general terms. The region is therefore Uttarakhand without the two circles of the garhwal-kingdom dossier (the pages name the Alaknanda, not the circles), which is why the confidence is 2. The Garhwal Kingdom page dates the British annexation to 21 April 1815; this dossier keeps the treaty's ratification. Reviewer sa-06-x, 2026-10-25: the first version drew the whole of Uttarakhand. The Terai strip east of the Mechi is drawn without Sikkim, Darjeeling and Kalimpong, as in the kingdom-of-sikkim dossier.

OVERLAP TO RESOLVE: Cliopatria's 'British Empire' row (slug british-empire, 1757-1858, 41 shapes, 4.18 M km2 at most; group sa-06, another part) is the same land as this dossier's gains: its shapes begin at 1762 with Bengal and grow to the 1856 maximum, with stray Canadian cells in the 1788-1821 bbox. Page budget: the batch brief says 2-5 pages per state; this dossier opened 26 pages (25 used, 'Conquest of Sindh' loaded the Arab conquest article and was set aside) because the group scope asks for the Company's gains year by year from 1757 to 1857 and no single page carries them: Company rule in India, Subsidiary alliance and the Doctrine of lapse give years only; the war pages give the cessions.

Start and end: the Company was chartered on 31 December 1600 and dissolved on 1 June 1874; this dossier covers the Company as a ruler in South Asia, from 1600 (the charter; first land is the Surat factory of 1613, so the 1600-1612 core is a reading) to 1 November 1858 (Crown takes over). The VOC dossier (dutch-east-india-company) sets the precedent of starting at the charter. type is 'state' because the Company page calls it 'a sovereign power'; family britain.
